concept.name: Hidden Markov model
concept.definition: A probabilistic model in which an unobserved finite-state Markov chain generates observable emissions whose distribution depends on the current hidden state, specified by initial-state, transition, and emission probabilities. Rabiner's (1989) tutorial standardized its three canonical problems: evaluation, decoding, and learning.
concept.intuition: You cannot see the weather directly, only whether people carry umbrellas; from the umbrella sequence you infer the hidden rainy-or-sunny sequence, given how states persist and how each state produces observations.
concept.mechanics: The forward-backward algorithm computes the likelihood of an observation sequence and posterior state probabilities; the Viterbi algorithm decodes the most likely hidden state path; Baum-Welch (EM) re-estimates transition and emission parameters. In financial time series the emissions are typically Gaussian or Student-t densities on returns.
concept.formula: lambda = (A, B, pi): A = [a_ij] with a_ij = P(s_{t+1} = j | s_t = i); B = [b_j(o)] with b_j(o) = P(o_t = o | s_t = j); pi_j = P(s_1 = j).
concept.failure_modes: EM converges to local optima, so results depend on initialization, and the number of states must be chosen heuristically. The geometric state-duration distribution implied by a first-order chain may not match real regime persistence.
concept.misconceptions: That the Viterbi path equals the sequence of individually most probable states: they can differ, because Viterbi maximizes the joint probability of the whole path.
concept.example: A two-state Gaussian HMM on daily returns separates a low-volatility drift state from a high-volatility drawdown state, and Viterbi decoding yields a hidden regime timeline used as a trend filter.
